items.title: How Chicken Took Over The American Diet
items.description:
Americans eat about 103 pounds of chicken per person every year, which is roughly one chicken every five days. But how did chicken become such an important part of the American diet? The rise of the modern chicken industry involved thousands of years of history, wartime meat shortages, government-sponsored breeding contests, industrial farming, fast food, and even a bizarre Twitter feud.

In this episode of Weird History Food, we trace the surprising history of how chicken went from a relatively
items.why_watch: This traces chicken's unlikely rise from barnyard afterthought to America's dominant protein — covering the 1940s government breeding contests that engineered the modern broiler, wartime rationing that pushed beef and pork off the table, and the fast food industry that sealed the deal. At under 16 minutes, it's a surprisingly rich piece of food-system history that reframes something you probably ate this week.

In this video I'll talk about Research Rabbit - a new tool which uses AI to help you discover relevant and interesting research articles, tailored specifically to your inter
items.why_watch: ResearchRabbit is a free tool that maps academic papers visually — showing you what a key paper cites, what cites it, and clusters of related work you'd otherwise miss through keyword searches alone. Artem walks through a practical workflow rather than just demoing features, which makes this genuinely useful for anyone who regularly needs to get up to speed on an unfamiliar field or literature.

global_silver_linings.title: Pakistan Combines River Dolphin Sanctuaries Along the Indus River, Protecting 250 Miles of Habitat
global_silver_linings.snippet: Pakistan has created a wildlife sanctuary along 123 miles of the Indus River where it’s estimated 440 of these extraordinary freshwater cetaceans live. The endangered Indus River Dolphin has seen large declines in the amount of river it’s able to access as Pakistan’s economic growth drove river infrastructure projects like dams and irrigation canals. Some […] The post Pakistan Combines River Dolphin Sanctuaries Along the Indus River, Protecting 250 Miles of Habitat appeared first on Good News Network .
global_silver_linings.reason: Pakistan has united its river dolphin sanctuaries into a continuous 250-mile protected corridor along the Indus, giving one of the world's rarest freshwater mammals a real fighting chance at recovery. It's a powerful reminder that governments can choose wildlife over short-term convenience.

global_silver_linings.title: Life after: oil
global_silver_linings.snippet: Former oil executive Samantha Cooper once helped power the industry. Now she’s fighting to end its hold on our future The post Life after: oil appeared first on Positive News .
global_silver_linings.reason: Communities once defined by fossil fuel dependence are finding new identities and livelihoods on the other side of that transition, proving that economic reinvention is genuinely possible. These stories of resilience matter because they make the path forward feel less abstract.

global_silver_linings.title: An Ohio principal lost his job in 2024 for helping a homeless student. Then he adopted him.
global_silver_linings.snippet: The educator of 31 years and the student are finally sharing their side of the story. The post An Ohio principal lost his job in 2024 for helping a homeless student. Then he adopted him.
global_silver_linings.reason: A principal who risked his career to support a homeless student didn't stop there — he opened his home and his family to him permanently. It's a quiet, radical act of love that shows one person's commitment can entirely change the course of a young life.

global_silver_linings.title: Want to See a Tiger? Let These Women Be Your Guides
global_silver_linings.snippet: It is dawn in Tadoba-Andhari Tiger Reserve in the western Indian state of Maharashtra. Most of the tourists waiting to start their safari have come to see a tiger. Instead, another sight catches their attention: women in khaki uniforms climbing aboard the jeeps.
global_silver_linings.reason: Women from local communities are stepping up as tiger safari guides, bringing an intimate knowledge of the land that enriches the experience for visitors while securing meaningful work for themselves. Conservation and community empowerment rarely look this good together.

global_silver_linings.title: The case for eating blueberries every day, according to a nutritionist
global_silver_linings.snippet: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM There’s a specific kind of health advice that asks a lot of you: meal prep, supplements with confusing ingredient lists, routines that cost more than they should. Blueberries aren’t that. They can be inexpensive, they need almost no preparation, and the research keeps giving you more reasons to eat […] The post The case for eating blueberries every day, according to a nutritionist first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .
global_silver_linings.reason: It turns out one of the most effective things you can do for your long-term health is also one of the simplest and most delicious — a daily handful of blueberries packs a quietly impressive nutritional punch. Good news that's easy to act on is the best kind.

discovery_articles.title: A Brittle Coating on a 2,200-Year-Old Roman Shipwreck Reveals How Ancient Sailors Kept Their Ships Afloat
discovery_articles.snippet: Traces of pine tar and beeswax preserved on the vessel reveal the painstaking techniques shipbuilders millennia ago used to protect their ships from the briny deep
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Beeswax and pine tar — not iron or magic — are what kept Roman hulls from quietly dissolving into the Mediterranean over two millennia ago. There's something quietly astonishing about a thin, brittle crust outlasting empires to tell us exactly how sailors once coaxed wood into defying the sea.

discovery_articles.title: At Least One in Four Former NFL Players Who Died Between 2016 and 2021 Had the Progressive Brain Disease CTE, Study Suggests
discovery_articles.snippet: The true prevalence of the neurodegenerative disease—which is associated with repeated head injuries—among the deceased football players might be much higher. CTE affects other athletes too, including hockey players, soccer players and wrestlers
discovery_articles.ferns_note: One in four is already a staggering number — and researchers believe it's likely an undercount, since only players whose families suspected something was wrong tended to donate their brains for study. The disease we can only confirm after death may be far more common among the living than anyone wants to reckon with.

discovery_articles.title: This American Commando Parachuted Behind Enemy Lines in Both the European and Pacific Theaters of World War II
discovery_articles.snippet: A direct descendant of Thomas Jefferson, Francis Lowell Coolidge was an agent with the Office of Strategic Services, a predecessor to the CIA. Read his goodbye letter to his wife, published here for the first time
discovery_articles.ferns_note: A man who carried Thomas Jefferson's bloodline wrote a goodbye letter to his wife before parachuting behind enemy lines — not once, but in two entirely different theaters of the same war. That letter, unpublished for nearly eighty years, is the kind of document that makes history feel unbearably close.

discovery_articles.title: Tennis Matches Are Heating Up, Literally. Here’s How the Court Became a Living Laboratory for Managing Extreme Temperatures
discovery_articles.snippet: The sport’s hard-court surfaces can reach some 30 degrees hotter than the surrounding air. With elite players suffering heat illness on the world stage, athletes are following personalized cooling plans
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Hard tennis courts can run thirty degrees hotter than the air above them, essentially turning elite athletes into subjects in an unplanned heat experiment watched by millions. The sport is quietly becoming one of the sharpest real-world laboratories we have for understanding how human bodies cope with a warming world.

discovery_articles.title: A space telescope was falling from orbit. Its rescue mission fell apart too
discovery_articles.snippet: NASA’s attempt to save the falling Swift telescope failed, revealing the realities of the burgeoning field of satellite servicing.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: NASA's Swift telescope had survived nearly two decades in orbit, only to face its quietest crisis: a slow, unglamorous fall back to Earth that a rescue mission couldn't stop. It's a sobering glimpse into how the promising new field of satellite servicing collides with the blunt realities of orbital physics and logistics.

discovery_articles.title: Monkeys hunt small animals when fruit is scarce
discovery_articles.snippet: Capuchins hunt and eat small vertebrates more often as plant foods wane. The behavior may help us learn more about humans’ early dietary evolution.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Capuchin monkeys don't just opportunistically snatch prey — they ramp up hunting with almost deliberate strategy when fruit runs low, mirroring a flexibility that may echo in our own deep evolutionary past. The implication is quietly radical: meat-eating in early humans may have been less a preference than a pantry problem.

discovery_articles.title: Lush Foliage Permeates Xanthe Burdett’s Delicate Portraiture
discovery_articles.snippet: For Xanthe Burdett, the boundary between humans and nature is thin, malleable, and always in flux. Do stories and artists like this matter to you? Become a Colossal Member today and support independent arts publishing for as little as $7 per month.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Xanthe Burdett paints faces the way forests actually feel — as though leaves and skin are simply two expressions of the same patient, growing thing. Her portraits don't place humans in nature so much as suggest we never quite left it.

discovery_articles.snippet: When it comes to felines, the artist revels in "the contrast between how ordinary and how weird they are." Do stories and artists like this matter to you? discovery_articles.ferns_note: Minyoung Kim captures the peculiar truth that cats manage to be utterly mundane and profoundly alien in the same languid stretch. Her paintings treat that contradiction not as a puzzle to solve but as the whole delightful point.

featured_read.title: How Much of a Problem is AI’s Water Use?
featured_read.snippet: It depends. Though water consumption by data centers pales in comparison to that of some other industries, it’s a problem in water-stressed regions. Water-saving cooling technologies could help The post How Much of a Problem is AI’s Water Use?
featured_read.blurb: The question isn't whether AI is thirsty — it's whether it's thirsty in the wrong places, and this piece traces exactly how geography turns a manageable industry habit into a genuine local crisis. A clear-eyed look at the gap between global statistics and the reality on the ground in water-stressed communities.

reading_room.title: The Seniors Against Senior Housing
reading_room.snippet: "America’s elders need more places to live, but even in liberal enclaves that recognize the problem, developers are facing the fiercest foes of all: America’s elders."
reading_room.blurb: The sharpest irony in American housing policy may be this: the generation most harmed by the shortage of senior homes is also the one showing up loudest to block new ones. A portrait of how self-interest, fear, and neighborhood identity collide in the most unexpected of NIMBY battles.

reading_room.title: NASA Has Begun the Countdown to the Launch of the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope
reading_room.snippet: The new space telescope will help astronomers unravel the mysteries of the universe The post NASA Has Begun the Countdown to the Launch of the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope appeared first on Nautilus .
reading_room.blurb: Named for a pioneering astronomer who was denied credit for her own discoveries, the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope carries both a corrected legacy and a genuinely staggering mission — this piece sets out what it's going to look for, and why the answers matter.

reading_room.title: You Can Never Go Home Again. But You Can Spend a Lifetime Trying
reading_room.snippet: 'My father designed two of the houses I grew up in. Then he died. I’m still untangling where his taste ends and mine begins."
reading_room.blurb: When your father was the architect of your childhood homes — literally — grief becomes a design problem: which corners of your taste are truly yours, and which are just his blueprints still running in the walls. A quietly devastating essay about inheritance, loss, and the rooms we can never quite leave.

garden_note.note: Late August in Zürich carries that bittersweet richness — the days are still generous, but the garden is beginning to exhale, heavy with harvest and a faint whisper of autumn in the evening air. Tonight, step outside after supper and let the full moon cast its silver light across the bean rows and ripening apples; it is one of summer's last truly luminous gifts.
